transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Um, well, what brings me in is that my sleep has just gotten really, really messed up lately. I mean, it's completely out of whack. I work as a bookkeeping clerk, and you know, you really need to be sharp for that, looking at numbers and reconciling accounts all day, so I really need my rest. But lately, I'll go to bed and I just... I'll either stay up half the night with my mind just running and running. Like, I absolutely cannot turn it off. I'll be thinking about spreadsheets, or errands, or just random conversations, and I'm just staring at the ceiling for hours. 

Or, if I *do* manage to fall asleep at a normal time, the exact opposite happens. I'll wake up way, way too early, like 3 or 4 in the morning, and I'll just be lying there in the dark feeling like I never even rested at all. It's just so frustrating because I'm trying to do everything right, you know, to get a good night's sleep, but my brain just won't cooperate with me. I'm just lying there either wide awake at midnight with my thoughts racing or wide awake before the sun comes up feeling completely unrefreshed, and it's just making everything so difficult...
Over the past couple of weeks, have you been feeling down, sad, or have you noticed a loss of interest or pleasure in things you normally enjoy?

Yeah... um, actually, yes. It's, it's been really bad. Lately, I just wake up with this... this incredibly heavy, just completely empty feeling. It’s like a physical weight right in the middle of my chest. And it doesn't make any sense because, well, I'll just be sitting there in my living room in the morning, and I look around at my own condo—which, I mean, I worked *so* hard for. I started working right out of high school, doing all these different clerical jobs, saving literally every penny I could while everyone else my age was out spending their money, just so I could finally have my own place and be independent. 

And I did it, you know? I got it, and I painted it, and I set it all up perfectly. But now, even just sitting in this beautiful space that I earned, it just... it just makes me want to cry. I'll literally just be sitting on my couch and the tears will start falling and I can't even really tell you why. It's just so heavy all the time. And because of that, I haven't even really wanted to do anything I normally enjoy. Like, I usually love organizing my space or maybe doing a little baking on the weekends, but lately I just sit there with that awful, empty feeling, just wanting to cry instead of actually doing anything.
How long have you been feeling this way—experiencing that heavy, empty feeling and the loss of interest in activities you used to enjoy?

Well, um, if I really sit and think about it... it’s been a while. It’s not just a recent thing. This... this depressed, guilty fog has been hanging around for about five months now. Five whole months. And it’s just so confusing because, well, it actually got *much* worse right after I bought the condo. 

You’d think that would be the absolute happiest time, right? Getting the keys, finally having my own name on a deed after saving for years and years, working all those long shifts. But instead of being happy, I just remember moving my boxes in and this heavy cloud just completely settled over me. I kept telling myself, you know, maybe it’s just the stress of the mortgage, or the packing, or figuring out the new utility bills—because obviously, being a bookkeeper, I obsess over the budget and making sure every single number lines up perfectly. But the budget is fine, the boxes have been unpacked for ages, and yet I’m still just stuck in this awful fog. 

Every single day for five months, just dragging myself through it, feeling so incredibly guilty that I’m not enjoying this huge milestone I worked so hard for. I mean, five months is a long time to feel like you're just walking through mud, and I just can't seem to shake it no matter how much I try to rationalize it or tell myself I should be happy...

Aside from when you're trying to fall asleep, do you find yourself worrying excessively about various things—like work, finances, or other everyday matters—during the day, and do you have a hard time controlling or stopping that worry?

Um, no, not really. I mean, you would think I would, right? Especially with my job and everything. Because I deal with money all day long, staring at ledgers and reconciling accounts, making sure every single cent is perfectly accounted for. And then, of course, I have my own mortgage now, which is a pretty huge financial commitment for someone my age on a single income. 

But actually, during the day... I don't really feel anxious or worried about any of that. It's not like my mind is spinning with all these 'what ifs' or stressing about paying the bills or messing up at work. It's actually kind of the opposite? It's more like... I just don't have the energy to worry. I'll sit at my desk at the office, looking at a spreadsheet, and instead of worrying about making a mistake, I'm just staring at the screen feeling like my arms weigh a hundred pounds and I just want to put my head down. 

So, no, I don't really have that uncontrollable worrying thing while I'm awake and trying to get through the day. It's really just at night when my brain won't shut off and the thoughts just run, like I was saying before. But during the actual day, the daytime hours, I'm not pacing around or biting my nails about everyday stuff or finances. There's no panic or racing thoughts then, just... just that awful, muddy heaviness I was telling you about. So yeah, I wouldn't say I worry excessively during the day at all.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight over these past five months?

Well, yeah, actually. Um, I mean, I don't really step on the scale very often because, honestly, who wants to do that? But I know something's changed because my work pants—the black ones I wear almost every day to the office, the ones I got on sale at that outlet mall right before I bought the condo—they're definitely looser. Like, noticeably looser around the waist than they were just a few weeks ago. 

And I guess it makes sense, because my appetite has just been... well, it's just been totally off. Like, I'll get home from work, and normally I'd make something sensible, right? Maybe a piece of chicken or some pasta. But lately, the thought of actually cooking, or even just eating a full meal, is just too much. It’s like chewing takes too much effort. So I just... I skip dinner a lot. Or, if I do eat, it’s just me sitting at my kitchen island, staring at my budget notebook—because I still check the numbers every single night, even though I know they’re fine—and I'll just eat, like, a handful of saltine crackers. Just dry crackers, right out of the sleeve, while I go over the columns of expenses. It’s not even that I’m trying to save money on groceries or anything, I just... I look at food and I just don't care. I don't want it. So yeah, I guess skipping meals and living on crackers is definitely making me drop some weight.
Did these sleep problems start around the same time as the heavy, empty mood you described five months ago, or did the trouble sleeping actually begin before that?

Well, um, it's funny you ask that, because I've actually spent a lot of time trying to trace it all back, you know? Like, trying to figure out the exact timeline of when everything started going wrong. Because when you're a bookkeeper, you're used to everything having a clear starting point, a date on a ledger, a specific transaction you can point to. But with this... it's a little blurrier. 

If I really think about it, though... I'm pretty sure the sleep stuff actually started first. Yeah, definitely before the heavy, empty feeling really settled in. I remember it was back when I was still in the middle of closing on the condo. It was maybe... gosh, maybe a month or so before I actually got the keys and moved in? So that would make it, what, six months ago? Six and a half? 

I just remember I was still living in my old apartment, the one with the terrible radiator that clanked all night, and I started having these nights where I'd just lie there, staring at the ceiling. And my brain would just be going a mile a minute. I'd be thinking about the mortgage paperwork, and whether the inspection would pass, and if I had saved enough for the closing costs, and just... everything. It was like my mind was a motor that someone forgot to turn off. And it wasn't just the condo stuff, either. Sometimes my thoughts would just jump from one random thing to another, like a pinball machine. I'd be thinking about a spreadsheet I was working on, and then suddenly I'd be thinking about a conversation I had with my sister three years ago, and then I'd be worrying about whether I left the coffee maker on at work. 

So yeah, the sleep problems definitely started before the depression. It was like this awful prelude, you know? The racing thoughts and the tossing and turning came first, and then, a month or two later, right after I finally moved into the condo, that's when the heavy, muddy fog rolled in and I just stopped caring about everything. So the timeline is definitely sleep issues first, then the mood crash.
Has anyone told you that you snore loudly, gasp, or stop breathing for moments while you sleep?

Well, no, not really. I mean, it's kind of hard to say for sure, right? Because I live alone now. When I was in my old apartment, I had a roommate for a couple of years—Sarah, we went to high school together—but she never mentioned anything like that. She was a super light sleeper, too. Like, she would wake up if I just got up to get a glass of water in the middle of the night. So I feel like if I was snoring really loudly or gasping for air, she definitely would have said something. She was not shy about complaining if something bothered her, believe me. 

But since I bought the condo and moved in by myself, there's obviously nobody here to tell me what I'm doing when I'm asleep. Or, well, when I actually manage to fall asleep, which, like I said, takes forever because my brain just won't shut up. But once I do finally drift off, I don't think I'm waking myself up by gasping or choking or anything like that. I don't wake up feeling like I can't breathe. I just wake up feeling exhausted, like I haven't slept at all, but I don't think it's because I'm stopping breathing. 

I actually read an article about that once, sleep apnea, I think it's called? Because my uncle has it, and he has to wear this giant mask thing to bed every night that looks like something out of a sci-fi movie. He said he used to snore so loud it would rattle the windows, and his wife finally made him go to a doctor because she was terrified he was going to suffocate in his sleep. But I don't have anything like that. I don't wake up with a sore throat or a dry mouth, which the article said were signs of it. I just... I just have the racing thoughts keeping me awake, and then the heavy, awful feeling the next day. So, no, nobody has ever told me I snore or gasp, and I really don't think I do.
During these past five months, have you had any thoughts of death, that you'd be better off not being here, or thoughts of harming yourself?

Oh, no. No, definitely not. I mean, I know I’ve been sitting here telling you how awful and heavy everything feels, and how I’m basically just sitting at my kitchen island eating saltines because I don't have the energy to care about anything, but... it’s really not like *that*. 

I don't want to die, and I definitely haven't thought about hurting myself. Honestly, I worked so, so hard to get where I am right now. I've been saving up for this condo since I got my first bookkeeping job right out of high school. Years of tracking every single penny, putting everything into these color-coded spreadsheets, skipping trips with friends just so I could finally have a place of my own. I wouldn't just throw all of that away. Even when the fog is really thick, and I feel like I’m just dragging my body through the workday, I don't actually want to not be here. 

It’s more like... I just want the heavy feeling to stop, you know? I want to be able to enjoy my life again, not end it. And as for hurting myself, gosh, no. The thought of getting hurt actually terrifies me. Like, I won't even buy one of those mandoline slicers for my kitchen because I'm so paranoid about accidentally slicing my fingers—not that I'm cooking right now anyway, obviously, but you get what I mean. I'm very risk-averse. It's the bookkeeper in me, I guess. We like things safe and balanced and accounted for. 

So, no, no thoughts of death or anything like that at all. I just want to figure out how to lift this awful weight so I can actually appreciate the life I’ve built, instead of just staring blankly at my ledger every night wishing I had the energy to do laundry. But yeah, no, nothing about wanting to die.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of sleep apnea (snoring, gasping, stopping breathing), which is not covered in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, no, not really. I mean, it's kind of hard to say for sure, right? Because I live alone now. When I was in my old apartment, I had a roommate for a couple of years—Sarah, we went to high school together—but she never mentioned anything like that. She was a super light sleeper, too. Like, she would wake up if I just got up to get a glass of water in the middle of the night. So I feel like if I was snoring really loudly or gasping for air, she definitely would have said something. She was not shy about complaining if something bothered her, believe me. 

But since I bought the condo and moved in by myself, there's obviously nobody here to tell me what I'm doing when I'm asleep. Or, well, when I actually manage to fall asleep, which, like I said, takes forever because my brain just won't shut up. But once I do finally drift off, I don't think I'm waking myself up by gasping or choking or anything like that. I don't wake up feeling like I can't breathe. I just wake up feeling exhausted, like I haven't slept at all, but I don't think it's because I'm stopping breathing. 

I actually read an article about that once, sleep apnea, I think it's called? Because my uncle has it, and he has to wear this giant mask thing to bed every night that looks like something out of a sci-fi movie. He said he used to snore so loud it would rattle the windows, and his wife finally made him go to a doctor because she was terrified he was going to suffocate in his sleep. But I don't have anything like that. I don't wake up with a sore throat or a dry mouth, which the article said were signs of it. I just... I just have the racing thoughts keeping me awake, and then the heavy, awful feeling the next day. So, no, nobody has ever told me I snore or gasp, and I really don't think I do.

inference.note: Ruled out G47.00 (sleep apnea) — no witnessed snoring, gasping, or breathing pauses, and no associated dry mouth/sore throat; prior roommate never reported such symptoms. Continued support for F32.9 given 5-month history of depressed mood, anhedonia, guilt, appetite/weight loss, and low energy. F51.0 retained since sleep-onset insomnia and early morning awakening preceded the mood episode by about a month, suggesting a possibly independent insomnia component.

doctor.intent: Assess for suicidal ideation or thoughts of death, a core MDD symptom not yet explored, to help confirm the depressive syndrome and rule out primary insomnia disorder as the sole diagnosis.
doctor.question: During these past five months, have you had any thoughts of death, that you'd be better off not being here, or thoughts of harming yourself?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about suicidal ideation or thoughts of death, which is not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Oh, no. No, definitely not. I mean, I know I’ve been sitting here telling you how awful and heavy everything feels, and how I’m basically just sitting at my kitchen island eating saltines because I don't have the energy to care about anything, but... it’s really not like *that*. 

I don't want to die, and I definitely haven't thought about hurting myself. Honestly, I worked so, so hard to get where I am right now. I've been saving up for this condo since I got my first bookkeeping job right out of high school. Years of tracking every single penny, putting everything into these color-coded spreadsheets, skipping trips with friends just so I could finally have a place of my own. I wouldn't just throw all of that away. Even when the fog is really thick, and I feel like I’m just dragging my body through the workday, I don't actually want to not be here. 

It’s more like... I just want the heavy feeling to stop, you know? I want to be able to enjoy my life again, not end it. And as for hurting myself, gosh, no. The thought of getting hurt actually terrifies me. Like, I won't even buy one of those mandoline slicers for my kitchen because I'm so paranoid about accidentally slicing my fingers—not that I'm cooking right now anyway, obviously, but you get what I mean. I'm very risk-averse. It's the bookkeeper in me, I guess. We like things safe and balanced and accounted for. 

So, no, no thoughts of death or anything like that at all. I just want to figure out how to lift this awful weight so I can actually appreciate the life I’ve built, instead of just staring blankly at my ledger every night wishing I had the energy to do laundry. But yeah, no, nothing about wanting to die.

inference.note: Insomnia symptoms appear temporally linked to and better explained by the depressive episode (racing thoughts, early waking, unrefreshing sleep coinciding with mood decline) rather than a primary sleep disorder; no evidence of sleep apnea (no snoring/gasping reported) or independent daytime anxiety/worry to support GAD. This effectively rules out F51.0 as a separate diagnosis, leaving Major Depressive Disorder as the primary diagnosis.

opening_question.intent: Identify the primary reason for the patient's visit today
opening_question.question: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with a 5-month history of persistently depressed/empty mood, anhedonia (loss of interest in organizing/baking), excessive guilt, significant appetite loss with unintentional weight loss, insomnia (both sleep-onset and early morning awakening), fatigue/low energy, and psychomotor slowing (heavy arms, difficulty completing tasks). These symptoms occur nearly every day for 5 months, causing functional impairment (reduced work performance, self-care, social/domestic functioning). No manic/hypomanic symptoms, no psychotic features, denies excessive daytime worry (against GAD), and denies snoring/gasping/apnea symptoms (against sleep apnea as primary driver). No suicidal ideation. This constellation meets criteria for a Major Depressive Episode; insomnia appears secondary to the mood episode given temporal overlap and symptom quality (rumination, not worry), making F32.9 the best fit rather than a primary sleep or anxiety disorder.
